section_1.title: Primes: The Atoms of Arithmetic
section_1.content: Introduce prime numbers as the building blocks of integers. Define the Prime Number Theorem visually: as numbers grow, the density of primes thins out at a rate of 1/ln(x).
section_1.example: Visualize a 10x10 grid of numbers where primes are highlighted in neon blue, showing the 'scattering' pattern becoming sparser as we zoom out.

section_2.title: The Pi Connection: Why do Primes and Pi converge?
section_2.content: Introduce the Basel problem and the connection between the Riemann Zeta function and prime distribution. Explain how the probability of two random integers being coprime is 6/π².
section_2.example: An animation showing a 'Random Rain' of integer pairs. If the dots are coprime, they turn green; the cumulative ratio of green dots eventually stabilizes around 0.607 (6/π²).

section_3.title: Dirichlet’s Theorem: Primes in Arithmetic Progression
section_3.content: Explain that primes aren't just random; they follow patterns in arithmetic progressions (a + nd). If a and n share no common factors, there are infinitely many primes of that form.
section_3.example: Imagine a 'Prime Detective' robot walking down a street with houses numbered 3, 7, 11, 15... The robot finds a 'Prime Treasure' in almost every house, proving the infinite distribution.

section_4.title: Synthesizing the Patterns
section_4.content: Summarize how these concepts transition from the randomness of individual primes to the deterministic global structures defined by Pi and Dirichlet.
section_4.example: A final visual overlay: A 3D graph showing the 'Prime density wave' superimposed onto a Circle, demonstrating that even 'random' numbers obey the geometry of the universe.
